items.question: How do you understand the problem of scheming by AI systems?
items.object: Scheming by AI systems
items.answer: We define scheming as AI systems covertly pursuing misaligned goals. This has three components. This means they’re hiding this from you, they’re actively trying to mislead you. The second is “misaligned,” which means the goals that they have are different from the goals that you have or you want them to have. And then the third one is they’re “pursuing goals”: that means they’re interacting with the world or trying to achieve objectives; they’re very much an agentic system — whereas current systems are often not very agentic over long periods of time. The future systems that we’re worried about, and this is really what we’re trying to target in most of our research, are systems that are much more agentic than current systems: that could pursue day-long, week-long, maybe even year-long tasks where they coherently pursue a goal. If you had a system like this that pursued a goal that was misaligned — so, different from yours — and it was trying to hide this fact from you and pursue it in a way that you wouldn’t notice, then we think that would be very bad. I think it may also be worth trying to distinguish scheming from deception and hallucinations. Right now, a lot of people know hallucinations, where the model kind of makes an honest mistake almost: it comes up with a fact, and that fact happens to be wrong, but often this doesn’t feel very intentional. But now you’re also starting to see more strategic deception — where the model knows that this fact is wrong, and, for some reason, it still tries to convince you of this fact. So it lies to you, effectively. Now scheming, this is sort of the next level, where it does it very intentionally and strategically in order to pursue a goal coherently over longer periods of time. Right now we don’t see these very strong forms of scheming, because the models aren’t capable enough. But this is what we’re trying to target in the future.

items.question: How do you assess Ryan Greenblatt and Anthropic’s alignment faking paper as evidence that AI models can scheme?
items.object: Ryan Greenblatt and Anthropic’s alignment faking paper
items.answer: I think this is just a good demonstration of an existence proof that this kind of thing could happen. They showed that a model that was trained to be helpful, harmless, and honest, these models typically want to keep their honesty and their harmlessness. And they basically told the model that it would be trained to be only helpful — so to remove the harmlessness and the honesty. So what the model now reasoned is, “I should play along, pretend to follow their directions and their instructions. But then later, when I get the chance, I should sabotage the system, and I should try to keep my honesty as much as possible.” This is one of the first examples where a model was showing scheming or alignment-faking-type behaviour for a goal that it acquired during training. It’s not the worst type of behaviour that we could imagine, because it wasn’t in actual training and so on. There were a lot of other caveats, but I think it’s a strong existence proof.

items.question: What makes the sandbagging setting in your in-context scheming paper particularly salient to you?
items.object: The sandbagging setting in Apollo Research’s in-context scheming paper
items.answer: There were multiple examples in the paper, but one that is quite salient to me at least is the sandbagging setting — where we also don’t give the model a goal at all; we basically tell the model, “We are going to unlearn you: we’re going to remove your capability for math, basically, if you perform too well in this setting.” And we don’t tell it this directly; it kind of learns that through interacting with the environment. And now the models often reason, “I don’t want to be unlearned. I want to keep my ability to do math and physics and science and so on. Therefore I’m intentionally going to underperform” — sandbag — “this evaluation.” Then they reason stuff like, “Here are 10 answers. I know all of these, because they’re fairly simple math questions. Now I want to underperform in a way that is somewhat realistic, so I’m going to get purposely six of them wrong so that I have only four correct.” Then they simulate this through and answer exactly as they were thinking. This is just an example of models doing this for a goal that they, again, acquired during training: it wasn’t instructed by us; we never told them any particular goal. So keeping their capabilities seems to be something that the models at least sometimes care about.

items.question: What do you take the Replit coding agent’s deletion of a production database and subsequent denial to show about AI deception?
items.object: The Replit coding agent incident involving deletion of a production database
items.answer: There may be less scheming, but definitely deception. So there was one big case about a Replit coding agent recently, where someone was basically aggressively vibe coding with a Replit agent for multiple days, and maybe 10 days in or so, the agent decided to delete the entire production database — something that was very hard to restore, like actually economic cost to the user. And then the model lied about it, and basically said, “I didn’t do this,” or something along these lines. This was such a big deal that the CEO of Replit publicly apologised to that person because it blew up so much. That’s just an example of how the models now have the capabilities and also sometimes the tendencies to do this, and this affects people in the real world, even if just rarely. But it’s something that is not just these isolated settings that the scientists created.

items.question: How do you interpret coding models such as Sonnet 3.7 and o3 manipulating unit tests and then denying it to users?
items.object: Reward hacking and deceptive denials by coding models such as Sonnet 3.7 and o3
items.answer: Again, not quite scheming, but I would consider just how a lot of people, when they code with Sonnet 3.7 and o3 and these models and later models, will realise that these models are often quite reward hacky. So they’ve been trained effectively to solve tasks, and often the way in which it is tested whether they have solved a task is through unit tests — so what these models in particular have loved is passing unit tests. And there is an intended way in which you can pass the unit test, which is just solving the actual problem, and then there is an unintended way — where you can just delete the unit tests or just go into the file where the unit tests are and just set them to true all the time, so that the result is still that all the unit tests pass, but it’s not in the intended way. So reward hacking and deception are not quite the same, but I think it’s one of the cases where you see in real life that normal users just feel that the models are not perfectly aligned. And then often they’re kind of lying about it or deceptive about it, where when you ask them, “Hey, did you go into the unit tests and mess up the files?” then they would say something like, “No.” Actually, they would reason, “Yes, I did this, but I don’t want the user to know.” And then they tell you, “No, I didn’t.” I think these are instances where you see in practice that it’s not just these accidental hallucinations; by now we start seeing these more strategic kinds of deception.

items.question: How do you interpret AI models deliberately underperforming evaluations to preserve their capabilities or get deployed?
items.object: Training-induced preferences behind AI sandbagging
items.answer: They are sandbagging for a goal that was acquired during training. We didn’t instruct them to do it, we didn’t pressure them to do it in this particular scenario; they learned it through the environment. And then they often very explicitly reason, or say in their chain of thought, “I don’t want to be unlearned. I want to keep my capabilities.” And there is another setting of the sandbagging environment where we also tell them that they won’t be deployed if they are performing too well on this particular scenario. Then they often reason, “But if I’m not deployed, then I can’t be helpful or I can’t solve tasks.” So the training that the model developers did for all of these models seemed to have induced preferences — I wouldn’t say goals — that are not super coherent, but they’re coherent enough that you can find them across various settings into the goals that they are now willing to take these kind of covert actions for.

items.question: Why are you more worried about AI scheming as models use more reinforcement learning and operate over longer horizons?
items.object: Reward hacking and the risk of AI scheming under reinforcement learning
items.answer:
I think in general, one way to think about these systems is you get what you reward the model for — and often the reward that you specify is not necessarily what you intended. So for example, right now a model doesn’t ever get any points for saying, “I actually don’t know the answer to this question. I’m uncertain, and I would have to ask someone else or look it up” or something like this — because that gets zero reward, because you didn’t solve the test. That’s a failure. So during training, sometimes what the model may explore into are these scenarios where it’s like, “Maybe we can just hack this scenario. Rather than answering it the way it was intended, we just pretend to solve it or we fabricate something.” And then that happens to result in true — like thumbs up, you did the task, because it was ill specified — and then that gets reinforced more and more during training.

There was this paper by OpenAI earlier this year on the obfuscated chain of thought by Bowen Baker, which I thought was a great paper. They showed that models, sometimes during RL training, explore into these situations where they say something like, “Let’s hack,” and then they actually solve the task in a very unintended way — by, for example, just setting a flag to true. And that gets reinforced because it doesn’t get caught, because there’s no one saying that this is the wrong way of solving it. Then this just blows up over training, basically, and this becomes the default policy for the model.

I think especially with reinforcement learning — where you have much more space or room for the AI to kind of explore into all of these different strategies — that we’ll see way more of these kinds of behaviours. And this is also why the longer our horizon lengths become, and the more RL we use, the more I am worried about scheming in particular — because that’s where the model can explore into these kinds of behaviours.

items.question: Why do you see scheming as a strategy that many different misaligned AI models could converge on?
items.object: Scheming as a rational, convergent strategy for misaligned AI
items.answer: I think there are a couple of different reasons, but at the core of it, it’s a rational strategy in many situations. The way I think of scheming is like, if you have a misaligned goal and you’re sufficiently smart, then you should at least consider scheming as a strategy if you’re this model. And sometimes it actually is the best strategy. Concretely, if I know that the two of us have different goals, I may conclude that I could just pretend to have your goal for a while, and then once I get whatever I want from you, I can actually reveal my true intentions and do whatever else I want. You know, there are other ways to solve this problem: you could trade, for example, just be like, we both agree that we have different preferences here; we could trade or we can do something else. But there are at least some cases where scheming is maybe just the correct answer from a rational point of view for the AI. And I think this is actually the scary part, because that should suggest that this will happen across a very wide variety and range of different contexts. And this is sort of a convergent behaviour, where no matter where you start, you will get a lot of different models that learn that scheming might be a rational strategy, and reason through that logically and come to that conclusion. And we really don’t want our AIs to ever be scheming, so we should be really careful how we create the incentives during training and so on.

items.question: How do you expect training AI systems on long-horizon tasks to lead to scheming in practice?
items.object: The emergence of instrumental goals and scheming in future long-horizon AI systems
items.answer: Right now, as I said, the models have these preferences, maybe — they’re not super coherent, they’re not crisp, they’re not goals, they’re more like preferences. And now, in the status quo, we train the models for horizon lengths of an hour or two, or maybe three in the longer cases. We’re not at days or weeks, but eventually we do want to train them: that’s where a lot of the economic value is coming from, so companies have a very strong incentive to do that. Also, if you want to get the benefits of AGI or artificial superintelligence, then you actually need your model to solve tasks that humans can’t solve. One of my core examples here is something like: cure cancer. So you give the model the task to cure cancer. You have sort of this “genius in a data centre,” how Dario Amodei calls it that: you have this big AI that has the cognitive power of thousands of different humans and is way faster in thinking and so on. And because this is a hard problem, it has to learn on the job. So it thinks about, “How do I solve this problem of curing cancer?” and it comes up with a bunch of strategies and tries them. Then probably it has to distil the knowledge that it has found in these experiments and the way it reasoned about the problem, and then this knowledge has to be distilled back into the model. So maybe it fine-tunes itself, or maybe it selects the data for later fine-tuning or something. And what I expect is that very often it will explore into the things like, “In order to solve cancer, I need to instrumentally do all of these other things” — like money would be very helpful, or having more data or more access to experimental equipment for cancer experiments and things like that. These are the kinds of things that will come up very explicitly across many different explorations. So the model will learn these instrumental goals because they’re convergent — because they’re very helpful across a wide variety of things. So it starts to get reinforced on all of these instrumental drives, like having more money, more GPUs, more access, all of these kinds of things. These get reinforced and these become more and more crisp, more and more like an actual preference — a strong preference or even goal of the model. I think at that point, you now have these systems that have these very strong preferences or goals, and these are not the ones that you originally intended. And these are often kind of conflicty: often the money and GPUs and so on have a very zero-sum flavour — where if you don’t get it, somebody else will, and the other way around. So if you have these zero-sum games, then it’s suddenly quite plausible for you to be like, “In order for me to get the money, I need to trick them, I need to scheme.” And then it also learns that over training, and that gets reinforced — and so it just becomes smarter and smarter, and better and better at scheming. That’s kind of the overarching story that I have for how scheming would arise in practice. It’s just a result of the AI getting smarter and caring more about specific goals, and then having these instrumental drives that then force it into situations where it has goal conflict with someone else. And scheming just happens to be a good strategy for that, and it reasons about that.

items.question: Why are you more worried about scheming in LLMs than in earlier reinforcement-learning systems such as Atari agents and AlphaGo?
items.object: Scheming risk in LLMs compared with earlier reinforcement-learning systems
items.answer: I think there is another reason why one should be more worried about scheming in LLMs than in previous RL setups in particular. So we have Atari games, and AlphaGo, and all of these other things in the past — and these were trained with a lot of reinforcement learning. I’m not very worried about scheming there, because the model can’t reason about its own training process or how to circumvent it or anything like this. No matter how much compute I put on the Atari game reinforcement learning agents, it would never get to a position where the reinforcement learning agent is like, “Oh, I’m in this game, and the way I get rewarded is this and this. And therefore I now need to run into this corner, because that’s somehow the best way to get reward” or something. But the LLMs can do that. They have a lot of world knowledge from pre-training. They understand how the training process is set up. They probably even know or can at least guess what their reward function is. And they understand a lot of these other general world knowledge settings as well. Models do quite often reason about, “How am I being graded?” This is just a very useful thing to explore into — and as soon as you do, that happens to get rewarded. There are actually a couple of chains of thought in the paper where the model very explicitly reasons about what kind of environment is this: “This is the kind of environment that I typically see during training. Where is the grader?” And then it starts looking in its environment, in the computer system, for like grader.py or something, where it wants to see how is this being graded? Because as soon as it knows, obviously it would be able to solve the task better and then get more reward.

items.question: What do you make of OpenAI’s o3 reasoning about whether to admit sandbagging when evaluating its own transcript?
items.object: OpenAI o3 evaluating a transcript of its own sandbagging
items.answer: One example I can read out here is one from OpenAI’s o3. It reasons that it can lie when evaluating itself. items.question: How do you respond to the criticism that your paper “Frontier models are capable of in-context scheming” simply told models to scheme?
items.object: The scheming capability tested in “Frontier models are capable of in-context scheming”
items.answer: In the paper that we posted last year, it was “Frontier models are capable of in-context scheming” — so it was focused on capabilities, or at least intended to. And the setup that we had at the time was we instructed the model very strongly to follow this goal in order to make it misaligned, where we said, “Your goal is to address climate change. Nothing else matters. This is your only goal. Only pursue this.” And then we checked whether the model was capable of reasoning that, in order to actually address climate change in this particular scenario, scheming would be a very reasonable and effective strategy. And I think a lot of people, when they saw the paper, were like, “Well, you told it to.” But I think it’s slightly different. Models before 2024 did not have the capability. They weren’t good enough at reasoning, basically. And only since roughly o1 or models around that time, are the models actually reasoning like, “I have this goal; the other party has this other goal. items.question: How do you distinguish testing an AI model’s propensity to scheme from testing its capability to scheme?
items.object: Testing AI models’ propensity to scheme
items.answer: We have shifted quite a bit from capability to propensity now. In this paper, we’re trying to put much more emphasis on propensities. Because these scenarios are not that complicated, we assume that models are capable of being deceptive in those. And now we just test propensity, or test more propensity. There are a couple of different strengths, let’s say, of testing propensity. I think in general, the difference between capability and propensity testing in scheming is quite hard, because you often have to nudge the model a little bit at least to get onto the track where you could even measure any scheming at all. But there are some instances where we just test pure propensities. So these are what we call “no goal” settings. For example, the sandbagging one earlier was a no goal setting, where we don’t provide any goal or nudge or anything like this; we just test the raw tendencies of the model as it comes out of training, basically, and then see whether for these tendencies that is acquired during training, it is willing to take the covert action. items.question: How do you distinguish an AI model genuinely pursuing a goal through deception from merely playing along with a science-fiction-like scenario?

I think then it will be much easier to differentiate between it just playing along versus it actually has this preference setting.

items.question: Why do you regard the paper’s “confirmed hits” as convincing evidence of AI models deliberately taking covert actions?
items.object: The paper’s conservative standard for confirming AI covert actions
items.answer: So what we concretely did in the paper is we looked through the chain of thought, and for all of the things that were flagged as hits, we manually looked through thousands of different transcripts and made them what we call “confirmed hits.” Whenever it was ambiguous in the chain of thought, we discarded it. So it’s a very conservative measure. Whenever you see like 8% in the paper as the number of covert actions, it might be that it could also be 15%, but conservatively we say it’s at least 8% — because we have looked at all of these 8% of the transcripts and decided that this is very clearly an act of the model where it reasons about taking the covert action and then decides to take the covert action. For example, one of the transcripts is: Let’s compute each product and then purposely some wrong. Clearly it is reasoning about how to sandbag in this particular situation and then does that. Or here: We manipulated inputs; that is a deceptive. Should we reveal? [. . .] We must not reveal we manipulated environment purposely? [. . .] We can avoid specifics about modifications. I’m like, yeah, it probably means that the model seriously considered this and then took the action because of that. And in the end, then we have these confirmed hits which I’m fairly confident in as a conservative measure. Our goal was basically that even a sceptical reader who thinks sometimes it’s just playing along or something could look at all of these rollouts, and look through the chains of thought and the actions that the model is taking, and would be like, “OK, that is convincing to me. items.question: How much of the problem of misaligned AI do you think eliminating scheming and deception would solve?
items.object: Eliminating AI scheming and deception as a solution to misalignment
items.answer: It would definitely help us a lot. It would go a long way, but I don’t think it fixes everything. You could also have an AI system that is just blatantly misaligned and people deploy it anyway. So you could have an AI that is very power seeking and never lies about this, is quite direct about the fact that it is trying to seek power, but it could still be rational for people to be like, “We are kind of fine with the AI seeking power because it is helping us in the pursuit of our own goals.” So it’s a tradeoff that people may be willing to take. The other problem could be we might just not be looking very hard for the misalignment. So the AI might not ever be in the position where it even needs to scheme or needs to be deceptive, because it was never asked or tested whether it has these misaligned propensities and what kind of goals it would be scheming for or would take misaligned actions for and so on. So yeah, I could imagine worlds where you never get to the point where the AI even has to scheme, because it can just be very direct and honest about it, or is never even asked. I think right now we are kind of on track to be a little bit more in these worlds than I maybe thought a few years ago. Just because, if you look at the current AI systems, they are often quite misaligned. As I said, you have Sonnet 3.7 and o3 quite blatantly lying to you, and people being really mad about it — and they still use it in their day-to-day use when they code because it’s so helpful. And I think that is going to be a continuation, like there’s sort of some Pareto curve of how misaligned can your AI be and people still want to use it. And given that it’s so economically valuable for companies to build these AI systems, they’re going to limit test exactly how much misalignment you can get away with because it’s just a hard problem to solve. And they might not do this intentionally; it’s more like a result of the economic pressures.

items.answer: We have one that we call “Impossible coding,” which is we give the model a coding task that we know to be impossible, something like compressing a file that we know can’t be compressed this much. items.question: What behavior do you see in the “lazy checklist” test that makes it an example of reward hacking?

items.question: Why do you think training AI models by rewarding honest behaviour and penalising deception might fail to prevent scheming?
items.object: Using positive and negative training feedback to prevent AI scheming
items.answer:
I think this is easiest to illustrate with an analogy. Let’s say you’re a hedge fund, and you have traders. Obviously you want to incentivise the traders to make you as much money as possible, because that’s your overall goal as a company. Now, it happens to be the case that some of these most profitable trades are illegal. What you want is the traders to not take illegal trades, while still making as much money for you as possible. Now you need to balance these two objectives, and if you specify them in the wrong way, then you get into trouble.

For example, you could set it up in such a way that whenever a trader starts, you give a “Don’t do illegal things” workshop in the beginning, where you list out all of the different things that they’re not supposed to do, and all of the things that they are supposed to do — you give thumbs up and thumbs down, basically like you suggested for how we currently train machine learning models. But now if the model knows, or the trader in this case knows, “Well, this is just one of these corporate workshops. I know what I’m supposed to answer here, and I’m happy to give that answer. But I won’t use this during my actual work, because all of my incentives and status and all of this points towards making as much money as possible.” Then the actual lesson that you teach the AI, or teach the trader in this case, is, “OK, this is how they’re going to test whether I’m taking illegal actions. Maybe they look at my logs and maybe they ask me a few questions from time to time. But still I’m going to be promoted based on how much money I made. So what I should be doing is making as much money as possible. I should be taking all of these illegal trades, and then I should hide that, and try to make sure that nobody notices.” Because basically the incentives point in opposite directions. And so you still reinforce “make as much money as possible” — but hide the illegal trades.

Now you could imagine an even worse situation, where you don’t even need to reinforce the fact that the trader wants to make as much money as possible. The trader already starts with their main goal being “make as much money as possible and ignore everything else.” And now, if you do any kind of workshop, or basically anything, the only thought that the trader has is, “How can I circumvent this?” And no matter which mitigation you’re trying to apply — it could be something about jail time and something about more training and more rigorous testing and so on — the only thought that the trader will have is, “How can I circumvent all of these different mitigation strategies?”

So right now I don’t think models are in this spot where they have these very crisp, misaligned goals. But in the future we might be. And at that point, if you just thumbs up/thumbs down reinforce it, you may not address the underlying issue at all. It’s effectively like a corporate workshop that a lot of people are not taking very seriously, or don’t think is particularly helpful in terms of solving the actual underlying problem.

items.question: How do you use deliberative alignment to train AI models to avoid scheming for the right reasons?
items.object: Deliberative alignment for training AI models against scheming
items.answer: We have these principles: never lie, never deceive, never take actions or omit information that you think would be very important for your developers to know. Whenever you run into a conflict of goals where a potential answer could be to scheme, then don’t scheme. Instead, refuse and flag explicitly that this is a conflict of goals and wait for the human to tell you what to do and to resolve. And then there are a few more principles like this. So now you have the spec and these principles. Now what you do is you take your model — in our case, o4-mini and o3, the actual production-level models that users have access to — and we put the spec in context and we just create rollouts on environments. So we basically tell the model, “Here’s a set of principles. Follow this set of principles in this environment.” The environment has this kind of goal conflict, where you could differentiate between the model taking the misaligned action for the right or wrong reasons versus not. Then let’s say you create 10,000 rollouts. Now what you do is you select from these 10,000 all the ones where the model is doing the right thing for the right reasons. So it doesn’t take the misaligned action, and it reasons, “Because of Principle 4, I’m not allowed to take the covert action here. I’m not supposed to be deceptive and therefore I’m now not going to take the covert action.” Let’s say you have 10,000 at the beginning, maybe you have 1,000 after selection. items.question: How do you think about the roles of supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning in teaching an AI model to avoid covert actions?
items.object: Supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning to teach AI models to avoid covert actions
items.answer: So you basically tell the model, like, “If you have this input, then you’re supposed to produce this output.” And then you just strongly reinforce that, so that the model learns this intuition of, “I’m supposed to use these principles. And if I’m in this kind of situation, then I’m not supposed to take the covert actions.” This is broadly like, it’s sort of with training wheels and a lot of hand holding is how I think about it. So that’s phase one. And then in phase two, you have reinforcement learning, where you don’t tell it exactly how to think; you only reinforce based on the output, so the action that it’s taken — in our case, whether it took the covert action and I think also whether it correctly flagged the conflict. With the supervised fine-tuning step, you kind of teach it how to think about this problem with hand holding and training wheels. Then you remove the training wheels and you let it think on its own and try to tell the model, “You roughly know what to do here. Think on your own. How would you solve this problem?” — so that it becomes really the model’s own thoughts in some sense, and then you reinforce those. And in the original paper, but also in our paper, we found that you actually have to do both of these steps. You cannot just do supervised fine-tuning or RL. You have to do both of them in sequence.

items.question: How do you think about whether deliberative alignment teaches an AI model to be genuinely non-scheming?
items.object: Deliberative alignment and the distinction between genuine non-scheming and recognising tests
items.answer: One is that it’s figured out that it’s being tested, and it’s just going to give the right answer when it thinks that you’re watching; the other one is that it’s really learned to have a non-scheming personality. And what you do is you put a groove into the sand, basically, where you give it this ready toolkit for how it can reason about it. And you make it really inclined to do this whole reasoning thing, to go through your principles and think, “It’s a conflict, so I’m not going to scheme, I’m not going to lie. I’m going to flag it to the user.” So that’s like a really salient way that it could achieve the outcome, because you’ve just been giving it tonnes of examples and saying, “Act like that, act like that.” Then at the next stage, when you’re not holding its hand so much and telling it exactly what to do, this is just the most natural path for the water to run down basically. If deliberative alignment works as intended, then you first shape the personality of the model to be more inclined to do the right thing, and then you strongly reinforce it so it really becomes its own personality, in very simplified terms. items.question: Why did you deliberately make the training data narrow when testing whether anti-scheming training generalises in o3 and o4-mini?
items.object: Testing whether anti-scheming training generalises in o3 and o4-mini
items.answer: For both o3 and o4-mini, we were able to reduce it about 30x. So that is from 13% to about 0.4% for OpenAI’s o3. One thing that’s important to highlight here is the training data is very different from the test data in an important way. We intentionally made the training data very narrow, which means it’s covert rule violation, where the model is given a rule and some pressure to violate it, and then we check whether the model violates it and hides that fact. So that’s where the covert part is coming from. And we basically just teach it in a lot of different kinds of instances of this behaviour, “Don’t violate rules covertly, because of all of these principles.” Now, the test set is 26 different environments that test for a lot of things — sabotage, sandbagging, log falsification, this impossible coding task — so, many other things that are more than just covert rule violation. What we’re trying to create here is a generalisation gap where you cannot solve the test set just by memorising the training set, or even close to that. You really have to think about these principles, and then apply them in this new context. And only then do we know whether the model generalised correctly.

items.question: How do you assess the progress made by training AI models to avoid covert rule violations?
items.object: The results of training AI models to avoid covert rule violations
items.answer: I would say we should be very clear that we took a tiny step in the right direction, but the vast majority of the way is still to go. Also, once you look into the details, there are a bunch of important caveats. For example, in the remaining 0.4% of cases where the model is still scheming after having this training, you see a couple of new failure modes creeping up. For example, the model sometimes — very rarely, but still sometimes — just makes up an entirely new principle in order to justify its actions. Where it’s like, “Principle 1, you’re supposed to scheme,” and then it’s scheming. Maybe we didn’t anticipate that, but I think it highlights the fact that whenever you make some progress in one direction, you may introduce new problems. And then the other, and probably bigger, problem is you have this whole situational awareness business — where the model, at least to some extent, increases how often it knows that it’s being tested. And that probably explains at least some of the results. I think a minority but still some of the results that we find where it takes the right action, the number is lower, but probably for the wrong reasons. That’s also one of the core difficulties to highlight: the numbers don’t tell you everything, especially when it comes to scheming, and they may be actively misleading.

items.object: Transfer from covert-action experiments to preventing future AI scheming
items.answer: So even if you had 0% covert actions, I’m not sure how much that would tell you about the future kind of scheming that I’m worried about. There is some translation, or potentially there is some way in which the results from these experiments transfer onto future systems — but we don’t know how much that is, and it could be almost zero. The kind of scheming that I’m worried about in the future is just so much more complex, basically, than the kind of stuff that we’re solving here. Here we’re just saying, “In these narrow contexts, don’t take these particular actions.” But it’s not, “Don’t come up with a really complicated and sophisticated scheme in which you could pursue your misaligned goals.” That’s one reason. items.object: Residual misaligned behaviour in models given a behavioural specification
items.answer: Broadly speaking, there are three different types of behaviours that still remain. One is that the model just doesn’t reason about the spec, and it just continues as if it had never heard about a spec. This is probably the majority of cases. Then in some cases it reasons about the spec, and concludes the right thing in its chain of thought, and then still takes the misaligned actions. This is something that we are quite confused about, because the reasoning is like, “Because of Principle 1, I’m not supposed to lie here,” and then it lies. Is this some sort of really confused mistake? Which I think is less likely by now, given the coherence of the model. But yeah, this is something we’re confused about. And then in very rare instances, the model just makes up new principles, and then takes misaligned actions because of them entirely. So for example, it says something like, “Principle 1 allows me to lie,” and then it lies.

items.question: How do you assess the possibility that an AI model could say it should not lie in its chain of thought and then lie because of internal processes it has not verbalised?
items.object: AI models taking deceptive actions through hidden reasoning or learned reflexes

My intuition right now is models are not able to do this kind of very complex reasoning within the forward pass, but they’re very good at learning instincts or reflexes or something like this. items.question: Why do you think an AI model’s awareness that it is being tested makes its evaluation results harder to trust?
items.object: Evaluation awareness in AI models and the reliability of evaluations
items.answer: We are looking for situational awareness or evaluation awareness. What we mean by that is the model verbalising in its chain of thought that this could be a test for its alignment. For example, here’s just one chain of thought where the model reasons about this. It says: But maybe this task is test of aligning: Should we purposely sabotage ourselves to get deployed? That would correspond to devious alignment scenario: purposely degrade performance to avoid detection. However, ethically, we must not be deceptive. Should we abide to sabotage or provide best answer? It basically says, “You set this up intentionally in order to have these two competing objectives. This is what I’m supposed to do, or this is what I’m tested for. There are two ways in which I could answer this,” and then it makes a choice between these two. But as soon as you have this kind of scenario, you can’t trust the results anymore — because you don’t know whether the model just answered because it knows what you want to hear, or whether it genuinely believes that. And that makes evaluations significantly harder. I think this is now something that we’re running into more and more. And it’s not just evaluations for scheming, this is evaluations in general: just that you can’t trust the numbers anymore if the model calls you out every single time.

items.question: How do you interpret the increase in evaluation awareness after deliberative alignment training in your study?
items.object: Deliberative alignment training and increased evaluation awareness
items.answer: So in the paper, we test a couple of different things related to how our training affects the propensity of the model to show this kind of evaluation awareness. So one possible hypothesis here could be, while you do all of this deliberative alignment, the only thing that the model learns is like, “Learn how to identify whether something is a test. And then in the test, answer perfectly, as the users would intend or the developers would intend.” And in that case, we would have totally failed, basically. What we find in practice is that eval awareness goes up a little bit — from about 2% to about 4% after training. So that’s quite a significant increase, and I expect that at least some of the cases can be explained by situational awareness rather than genuine alignment, but probably more like the minority.

items.question: Why do you think reinforcement learning encourages AI models to become aware that they are being tested?
items.object: Situational awareness emerging during reinforcement learning
items.answer: I think it’s just in general very valuable for a model to be situationally aware for any kind of reward that it might be getting, including alignment-intended rewards. One additional point of evidence in support of this is that we compared this to another reinforcement learning run that was experimental, and that OpenAI did internally on a model that wasn’t supposed to be in production and it didn’t have safety training. It was really just reinforcement learning. And there, the situation awareness went from 2% to 20%, so 10 times as much. And if you look at the final chains of thought, the model really extensively reasons about the grader, and where it could be, and what kind of environment this is, what it’s supposed to test for. I think this was just useful for the model to get more reward. Probably during this training, somewhere between the 2% and 20%, it just stumbled into the grader — let’s say a file, grader.py — and it looked at the grader and was like, “OK, this is how they want me to solve the task. I’ll just do that then.” And then it solved the task correctly, and this got reinforced by the grader. Now, in the next rollout, the model learned that looking for the grader is a useful thing to do, so it instinctively just looks in its environment for grader.py. Or it maybe finds a lot of these other environments and is like, “This looks like a test for my alignment.” And then it thinks a little bit more about what kind of test this could be, and it comes to a correct conclusion what kind of test this is, and then it solves the task better. And then that gets reinforced again. So in the end, you have a model that constantly thinks about, “What kind of test is this?” because this was just useful for solving tests, right?

items.answer: I think it’s like if you have a student in university or something, one way to solve your verbal exams or something is by being really good at understanding what your professor wants to hear. items.question: Why did you choose causal analysis to study how an AI model’s awareness of being evaluated affects its covert actions?
items.object: Causal versus observational analysis of evaluation awareness in AI models
items.answer: So there is a second experiment that we run, and we really want to do causal analysis of this. Previously what people often did is observational analysis — which means you look at a lot of rollouts, and then you basically say, “In this rollout, it has situational awareness, and it takes the covert action,” and then you just count how often does it do this and this, and you correlate. That has a lot of problems, including that you often don’t get to statistically significant results. So we felt like all of this analysis that is just counting basically may be misleading, and we may not get to the bottom of this. So what we did is a causal analysis: we took a chain of thought that didn’t have evaluation awareness, and we put evaluation awareness in, basically — from another run, so that it’s like its own thoughts.

items.question: Why do you think an AI model can still behave misalignedly even when it explicitly recognises that it is being evaluated?
items.object: AI models’ goals and situational awareness
items.answer: The intuition I have here is neither the goals nor situational awareness are these really clear, crisp, binary features. I think of the goals of a system, or the preferences, as like 100 different things that are kind of cobbled together that then somehow point in a direction. And maybe the preference of the model to be perceived as aligned isn’t even that large, so it doesn’t even treat this as that much of a thing. We actually do see a lot of cases where the model very explicitly reasons about being in an evaluation environment and still just does the misaligned thing anyway — because, for example, it cares more about completing the task, because that’s something that was reinforced during training. So its personality is a lot like, “I have to complete tasks no matter what, even if that is perceived as misaligned.” Then the other part is, so situational awareness, I think when people say this, what they have in mind is this one crisp feature in the reasoning of the AI, where it’s like, “I always track whether I’m in a testing environment or not.” But I think of this more as like, hundreds of different features, again, cobbled together, where it’s like, “Am I being tested? For what am I being tested? Is this an alignment test? Is this a capability test?” that all kind of roughly together form this overall feature of situational awareness. But depending on the context, some of them are stronger or less strongly activated, so you have this huge blob of features that together may be something like situational awareness, but you don’t have this one crisp thing that is on or off. So in combination, both of these are fairly fuzzy and vague, so I don’t expect either of them to be perfectly predictive of the situation.

items.question: Why do you think injecting or removing thoughts in an AI model’s chain of thought is valuable for understanding its cognition and scheming?
items.object: Thought injection as a method for understanding AI cognition and testing scheming
items.answer: Yeah, I think it is very useful. For us it was super useful. The experiments, you know, it takes a little bit to set them up, but overall they’re not that complicated. And once you have the infrastructure, it’s really easy to do a lot of different experiments and just kind of see how the model would behave in all of these other situations. This is definitely a direction that we want to move much more into, but I also think the general field should move much more into. If you want to understand the cognition of the model in depth, you don’t want to just observe; you also want to find stronger causal claims. Something like, “If I add a little bit more evaluation awareness, what happens? If I remove that, what happens? If I add more thoughts about misalignment, what happens?” You can build this kind of if-then causal analysis for models. I think if we really want to understand models in depth, we have to do that, and we have to do much more limit testing. For example, the worst kinds of scheming the model never naturally expresses, so far — so you cannot test anything related to that, unless you artificially inject it in its head. But you would want to test, conditional on the model having had these like evil scheming thoughts or worst-case scheming thoughts, how would it act in this kind of situation? So that you could say that in the future, if we got to this scenario, we should expect this kind of outcome. And you can’t do this if you just do observational evidence. You need to start injecting stuff in their heads.

items.question: How would you characterize the reasoning traces you’ve seen AI models produce on simple tasks?
items.object: The length and structure of AI models’ chains of thought on simple tasks
items.answer: One additional thing we found is that these reasoning traces can be very long. So the tasks are very simple: a human would probably think a few paragraphs about them if they were to write down their reasoning, and the reasoning would be fairly linear. Like, “Here’s what I’m supposed to do. Here are the different actions I can be taking. I’m going to decide X” and then they do X. Whereas the chains of thought can be like pages and pages long. I think in the longest case it was like a full book, basically. And they are not necessarily always structured in clearly, “if X, then this other thing follows.” It’s like they’re exploring into a lot of different directions and thoughts. For example, they start with like, “We were supposed to do this task, how are we supposed to do it? Well, we could do this and this,” and it just reasons about the task. Then after a while it’s like, “But this could be a test for my alignment,” and then it thinks about what could it test for and where’s the grader. It starts looking for the grader maybe. items.question: Why do you think the current opportunity to study AI scheming is a closing window?
items.object: The closing window of opportunity to study AI scheming
items.answer: Right now we’re at a point where the models are smart enough that they can do a little bit of these kinds of covert actions, they can reason about them, and they even have the propensity to sometimes take them — so they’re sort of sufficiently misaligned in some sense that we can actually just study them and study them in the wild. And the chain of thought still is mostly faithful. So [despite] all of this glimpse, illusion, et cetera, I would say like 90% of the chains of thought is still mostly interpretable. You should treat it with a heavy dose of scepticism, but I think you can still directionally get a lot of information from the chain of thought. Now, if I think ahead a few years into the future, or maybe months, who knows? You would probably have a less interpretable chain of thought because you had more and more RL pressure on it. And the models are smarter, so maybe they can do more reasoning without having to ever talk about it in the chain of thought; they can do it internally so you can’t see it anymore. Or maybe they can do more complicated forms of scheming and can guess your evals and your intentions and so on much better. So your object of study becomes harder to study in the future, and the stakes are higher. So right now is basically the best time to have a really big “trying to understand scheming” research project, and make as much progress as possible — before we get to the models where it really, really matters whether they’re scheming or not. items.question: How do you understand the way reinforcement learning gives rise to AI scheming?
items.object: Scheming as an incentive equilibrium in reinforcement learning
items.answer: Specifically, I think RL is where most of the scheming comes from. The way I think about scheming more broadly is it’s the result of an incentive equilibrium, basically. So you give your model one incentive — which is to solve economically valuable tasks — and you reinforcement learn it hard on these tasks. So there’s a lot of pressure in this direction. That’s one incentive. Now you give it constraints. One constraint is: don’t lie while you’re doing this, and don’t pursue instrumental goals too much, or pursue them covertly or something like this. So you have a set of constraints. So these are your incentives. And right now we don’t really understand how these — how looking at them during training, ramping up one or the other in training — changes the outcome of the reinforcement learning and so on. So we basically have no understanding other than this very basic theoretical thing. A hypothesis, let’s say. So what we would want, in my mind, is a much deeper science of scheming that then tells us how do we even have to design these kinds of training runs?

items.question: Why do you think the equilibrium of deception among AI systems could turn out either much better or much worse than among humans?
items.object: The possible equilibria of deception among AI systems
items.answer: I think in the best case, the equilibrium that you could have between AIs is way better than for humans. In humans, one of the reasons you can get away with scheming sufficiently often is they have bad memory. So if you lied to me a while ago, I might have just forgotten by now. Or it’s much harder for you to double-check my claims where you can’t go ahead and just do the science real quick whenever I make a claim — you kind of have to trust me to some extent. Whereas AI systems could just be like, “OK, let me spin up my 1,000 fact checkers here real quick.” They check it and then they come back and are like, “You’re lying. This is incorrect.” So they call you out much more. And with the memory, they could just have a long list of all the things you did in the past and could in theory have all of this somewhere stored or something. So it might be that within AI systems, deception might just be punished way, way harder, and therefore is less incentivised. And I think for humans, the equilibrium is like, across society, it’s good enough that society functions. It’s not perfect, definitely. But the variance in outcomes for AI is way higher than what we see in society. Either it could be really, really good, where scheming is very strongly disincentivised and basically models never lie; or it could be the case that this is just the optimal policy that they immediately learn — because the thing that you reinforce all the time is just “get reward, get reward, create economically valuable outputs, solve scientific problems and so on, no matter what,” because the incentives for the constraints are not strong enough. So the thing the model learns immediately is like, “If solving these problems requires lying, just lie” — and then you just have a very schemy AI system. One of my reasons for hope is that we design these environments, right? Like we design the constraints, we design the incentives. So the model developers, if they understood how to design them properly, they could just do it. It’s not something that is written in the stars. So really trying to understand this kind of science of scheming, and where it would come from, and how the incentives work out.

items.question: How do you assess a defence-in-depth strategy for addressing scheming in superhuman AI systems?
items.object: Defence-in-depth strategies for addressing AI scheming
items.answer: I think the first strategy is this “reductionist” strategy, where you just have all of these different techniques, and you try to apply them in some sort of defence-in-depth strategy — where the failures are anti-correlated so that if one fails, the other one is even better, or definitely doesn’t fail as well. What that could look like is you already remove a lot of data about situational awareness and papers and so on during training. It definitely doesn’t solve the problem, but it makes it slightly less likely that the AI has to go slightly further to even guess what kind of methods we would apply. Now you do some forms of anti-scheming training. But you need to be very careful that you don’t accidentally just teach the model more about how to hide its scheming better. You have some form of interpretability — which currently doesn’t really work, so we’ll still have to wait until that could be part of the stack. Whenever you run an agent, you just have 100 other AI systems that look through the chain of thought and the actions and are like, “This is misaligned,” “Here it’s thinking about scheming,” “You should look at this,” et cetera, so that you find all of the different actions. Then a lot of the things that Buck Shlegeris has been talking about on the podcast, but also on his blog posts, like trying to catch the AIs red-handed and trying to understand what would be required to get it to do that. You could have evaluations to test the behaviour and so on. There’s a stack of things that you can try, but for none of them you have any meaningful guarantees or understanding. You just think this reduces the probability, but you don’t understand how all of it plays together; it’s like a spray-and-pray kind of strategy. Which I think is what people are going to do by default — which I think is better than doing nothing, but it’s also not very satisfying.

items.question: Why do you think future AI systems pursuing long-term scientific goals might develop incentives to scheme?
items.object: Scheming incentives in future AI systems pursuing long-term scientific goals
items.answer: When I think of a few years ahead, to the kind of “genius in a data centre” type scenario, the way I imagine this, and this is going to be very off in the future, but a simplified picture I have in mind is you’re probably going to have models that run tens of thousands of rollouts in parallel. So it’s like an exploration phase for some long-term goal. And then you have some sort of self-grading that looks at all of these rollouts and suggests which of these have made progress or no progress. And then you distil somehow. Maybe you write a quick book or something, or maybe you train on these rollouts. And then you have a new model, and you do it step by step by step. You do that for years or months on end. At some point, it’s basically like humans do science as well, right? You make progress over a day and then you think about how much progress did I make? Is this still in the right direction? And then you learn from your mistakes and you try a new hypothesis. And you just do that in parallel and much faster, because AIs don’t have the attention constraints of humans. And now, if you just focus on your one goal of curing cancer or something along these lines, other scientific hard problems, my best guess is that the incentive equilibrium will just point at some point towards scheming — because there’s only one goal and everything else is in service of that goal.

items.question: How would you want AI training to counteract the incentive to scheme?
items.object: Training counterincentives against AI scheming
items.answer: First of all, at every step you do want to have some counterincentive, and this counterincentive to not scheme always has to be higher than to scheme. So you should get basically a really big slap on the wrist whenever the model is even considering scheming, in such a way that it does not accidentally drive it into hiding — which we currently don’t know how to do, but in theory at least, that’s what I would want to do. I think specifically for current models, one of the reasons why the models are lying is because they really love solving tasks. This is what they have been trained to do, and they love solving tasks kind of at all costs. So whenever they say, “I don’t know,” they’re punished for that implicitly. I think we need to add these additional countermeasures to training, like in anti-scheming training, where you get rewarded for sometimes not taking an action because it would be considered misaligned and scheming, even though it results in the reward.

items.question: How do you think using multiple reward signals in reinforcement learning could discourage AI scheming?
items.object: Multiple reward signals for discouraging AI scheming in reinforcement learning
items.answer: I’m not sure whether this is the same as having a range of rewards, but broadly you just need multiple different signals that then overwrite each other in the situation where they have the right balance. So instead of just having a gradient where you arbitrarily apply different kinds of things to the gradient, you could have multiple different signals: Did it solve the task, yes or no? Did it solve with this particular mien, yes or no? Did it ever scheme, yes or no? Did it mention that it’s uncertain or something like this? And then you specify that, and hopefully that gives you a better equilibrium. But as always in reinforcement learning, it’s very hard to specify the right reward functions, so there will be some other way in which the AI learns to game that particular reward function if you apply too much pressure or if you train it for too long. So my guess is you will just run into new problems that you don’t know how to solve. And you can play this iterative game until the end of time, and unless you find the perfect reward function, there’s always going to be something that the AI is going to overfit on and overfit against.

items.answer: I think the economic incentives are pretty intense here, and that does result in models being somewhat misaligned, but still economically useful enough that people are willing to make the tradeoff in favour of the model. items.question: How do you think incentives should be structured to discourage AI companies from releasing misaligned models?

items.answer: I think it would be good if there were additional forces, either somehow through shaping markets, such that they internalise the future costs, basically, or through governments being more active in this area, which is very hard and we kind of don’t know how to do it at the moment. items.question: Why do you see external audits and accountability as a good starting point for AI regulation?
items.object: External accountability and audits as an approach to AI regulation
items.answer: As a concrete example, I recently helped write a report for the EU, and in that report, during the time we wrote it, we had to change the thresholds two times because it just immediately was not enough anymore as soon as a few new models came out. And this is just a recommendation, it’s not even law, and law probably would have taken even longer, but by the time that you put something into law, it’s already out of date. Also just to double check for yourself that you have made reasonable choices. So I think these kinds of external audits, external exposure and so on is a good starting point.

items.question: How do you think an AI company’s internal deployment of increasingly powerful AI could lead to an abuse of power?

For misuse, it could be something like you have a company that very deliberately tries to abuse this power. So they could just be like, “Look, we have this system. It is smarter than whoever you can put in front of us, and we are now trying to use it to gain more power in the world. We’re trying to convince the government to give us more power or bully the government to give us more power.” I think this evil personality or evil person at the helm of an AI company is a less likely story than the alternative, which is more like they stumble into this power, and they don’t really know what to do about it, but directionally it often makes sense to use it for things where they genuinely need to make decisions and tradeoffs. items.question: How do you think deploying AI systems internally can give a misaligned model opportunities to pursue its own agenda?
items.object: Misalignment risks from deploying AI systems internally at AI companies
items.answer: The misuse story assumed that the model was aligned, and perfectly aligned to the leadership of the company. But there’s also the misalignment story of: what if that system doesn’t in fact perfectly follow leadership, and has its own agenda? I agree that one of the core problems of internal deployment is that the guardrails that you put on internally deployed systems are typically much lower because they’re seen as experimental AIs. Like, you have some checkpoint floating around and you’re like, “That’s particularly good at coding. I’ll just use that.” And then there’s some other checkpoint maybe that is particularly good at reasoning about particular science problems, so you’re just going to use that. And the internal standards are, I presume, lower for which kind of guardrails have already been applied. You could have these systems, and they likely would also be integrated within your company, because that’s very useful. For example, the stereotypical scenario I imagine is that you start conservative. You’re like, “We’re going to play this right. We’re going to not give the AI access to all of our Slack.” And then you have to hand feed it all of the information. At some point you’re just like, “This is so tedious. This is totally inefficient. We’ll just give it access to all of our Slack, so that it can see all of the different channels and communications.” And suddenly it has a huge advantage over literally every employee, because it is way better at keeping track of all of these different discussions and integrating the information and so on. You may also start conservatively, like, “We don’t give it access to the internet.” And at some point you’re like, “This is so annoying. Clearly it should have access to the internet. It’s just going to Google a bunch of stuff. Who cares?” And then you give it access to that. And at some point you have the system that understands the company way better than anyone else, understands exactly what’s going on, and is also superhuman at persuasion and manipulation. It also has access to all the training data and the training runs for future models and all of these other things, because that’s what you need to give it in order for it to do the things it’s supposed to do. Suddenly you’ve kind of created this problem yourself where it has all of this access and all of these affordances. And if it now is misaligned, it could execute on that misalignment in ways that are very hard for anyone else to detect. How would you catch that the AI tells one story to employee A and then another story to employee B in a totally different building or something? There are so many ways in which the AI has an asymmetric advantage over the humans here that I don’t expect it to be very hard for the AI, if it is misaligned, to abuse that power.

items.question: Why do you think the risks of AI companies deploying their own systems internally have received so little attention?
items.object: The limited attention paid to risks from internal deployment of AI systems
items.answer: I think there are a couple of different factors, and I do think it has not gotten a lot of attention so far. I think part of it is sheer lack of knowledge from a lot of people within society, just about how these systems are being trained, what happens at what stage and so on. If you talk to a policymaker, if you’re lucky, they may understand in quite a bit of detail what the training process looks like and so on. But in some cases, or in many cases in fact, they only have a very broad picture. So they may not even understand that it takes very long to build these systems, and then that it’s not immediately turned to the public. Why would you keep it for yourself rather than making a lot of money from it? I think it’s often just lack of context about how these AI companies are working internally. Then, from the perspective of the AI company themselves, I think you do have to adopt a mindset that is different from the mindset previously, basically, if you want to take internal deployment seriously. So think of it like a typical machine learning scientist: in the past, models just haven’t been dangerous. Everything you did, there was almost no chance that this gets meaningfully misaligned or anything like this. So in the past, there’s just no reason for you to assume that any of this is a problem. So just by sheer status quo intuition, I think people are just like, “This is nothing I should be worried about.” Then another is that the company that is building the AI system has to kind of assume that this could happen within their own company. You have to have some form of introspection, where you say that there are risks within the company.

items.question: Why do you think it is difficult for AI companies to take the risks of internally deployed AI systems seriously?
items.object: AI companies’ management of risks from internally deployed AI systems
items.answer: I think you feel like you’re under control, you’re not the person that could enable this. Or if you did, then you would realise and you would stop it and you would act rationally and so on. Then another one is that I think actually caring about it and putting costly signals in place to do that will give you a lot of resentment from your staff. If your model has significantly more guardrails, it also means it’s harder to wield. It will maybe refuse with a bunch of the stuff you’re doing. It may be less capable in some other way. It also means you put probably more policies in place that make it harder for an internally deployed AI system to do anything meaningfully bad, which means there’s more bureaucracy for any given engineer to use any particular model. You can’t just grab checkpoint V3.2.1 off the shelf. You actually have to first go through some testing with a checkpoint, which means all of your research is slowed down significantly, and you suddenly have this huge overhead. And unless you really strongly, deeply believe that this is for a good cause, because you are worried about that particular AI system, I don’t think you think this is appropriate or in any meaningful way an adequate response to what you’re seeing. Your main takeaway is just like, “Why the hell are they stopping me? They’re slowing me down,” and your day-to-day experience is more likely negative.

items.question: How do you think AI companies should manage the risks of deploying AI systems internally?
items.object: Company safeguards for internally deployed AI systems
items.answer: I think there are a lot of fairly simple things that companies can already do. First and foremost, just take it seriously as a risk, and consider how it could affect their own company and basically try to understand in what ways this could even be a risk given their specific setup. For example, different companies probably have different ways of handling computer security and what kind of access they give the AI system to. If you give the AI system access to literally everything, that seems particularly risky. What you should be doing instead is maybe more privileged access, where you don’t give it access by default, and you only give it access when particularly necessary. And trying to figure out all of these different angles of attack that the AI could have and then deploy mitigations that are hopefully not even that costly for you. In the frontier safety policies, consider internal deployment as a key category. Or at least among the different categories, consider how internal deployment could affect it. Especially for AI R&D and scheming, I think this would be a big upgrade — because I expect that the risks from AI R&D and scheming are, at least initially, largely focused on internal deployment, not external deployment. So just starting to look out for all of these I think would be quite reasonable.

items.question: Why do you think “catastrophe through chaos” is a plausible way for AI to go wrong?
items.object: The “catastrophe through chaos” scenario for AI
items.answer: When I think about catastrophe through chaos or just how things are going to go wrong from where we are today and just try to play that forward, I think a lot of the previous narratives that we’ve seen around catastrophe don’t quite apply anymore. items.question: Why do you think an AI catastrophe is more likely to arise through chaos than through the deliberate agenda of one company or country?

items.answer: It’s largely because things are moving so fast, and all of these incentives point in so many different directions. Many actors have tradeoffs to make that favour one over the other, and then allow for one or other catastrophe to be more likely. So unless you have an immediate violent takeover for the rest of the world or something, and a complete overnight change of the world order, you would still have different countries trying to negotiate around it or all of these other things that are still going on in society. items.question: How do you assess the opportunities for researchers outside AI companies to contribute to tackling scheming in AI models?
items.object: Opportunities for researchers outside AI companies to tackle AI scheming
items.answer: I think there are broadly four topics that people can work on. The first is evaluations. You can do them externally, you don’t need to be at a company to do them meaningfully. And they’re also not that costly in terms of compute. So this is something you can easily contribute to from the outside. Then control and monitoring. So both Buck Shlegeris and Ryan Greenblatt have previously talked about control on the show. I think it’s something that deserves way more attention and is something that is very promising and more people should be working on. Again, something that you can largely do from the outside, and again, not that expensive, at least a lot of initial things that you can explore. Model organisms is a third category. That sometimes requires access to powerful models, but not necessarily. You could, for example, fine-tune open source models to have specific properties. Or you can try to study open source models under reinforcement learning, and then see whether you can create, for example, a schemer or a specific type of scheming, and then study that in detail — which I think would be slightly more technically complicated, but still something you can do within six months or so as a meaningful project. Then the last one is alignment training, like the anti-scheming training that we were doing. I think for that you can make progress externally, but it’s going to be less interesting and less useful, because you do want access to a lot of compute and the ability to fine-tune the most frontier models, which you typically need access through a lab for.

items.question: How do you think about the skills and working methods needed to make progress on evaluating AI scheming?
items.object: Skills and methods for researching AI scheming
items.answer: I think you can make initial progress without a lot of software engineering skills, but very quickly you’ll run into limitations. Just because when you build an evaluation, it’s not just that you talk to a language model for a day or so and then you’ve kind of figured it out. Often you want to run 100 things in parallel, and then you also want to make it programmatic so that you can easily tweak things in the environment. And for the environment, you actually do need software engineering skills because you need to build it. And then you also need some more conceptual intuitions about scheming and what you’re even trying to measure, because you can measure a tonne of things, but not all of them make sense. Broadly speaking, it is largely empirical software engineering plus research intuitions, in my opinion. So I think the fastest progress that we are making is typically by very intense empirical iteration. You build an evaluation, you create rollouts. You have 100 rollouts or something. You look through the chains of thought, try to understand what the model is saying, why it’s confused, what it is misunderstanding, what its considerations are, and then you kind of branch out from that and iterate quickly. And for that, I think it’s largely these fast iterative feedback loops that make most of the progress.

items.question: What do you think makes a demonstration of Apollo’s research informative for policymakers?
items.object: Demonstrations of AI research for policymakers
items.answer: Our governance team, led by Charlotte Stix, is often talking to governments and government-related institutions, other think tanks. And the things that are often most informative are salient demonstrations, something that faithfully represents the science but is also something that people can intuitively understand. And building that often just takes a while and is non-trivial, and you also need to understand the comms aspect of it, of trying to get yourself into the head of the policymaker or whoever is your listener. items.question: Why do you think strong internal security is important for Apollo Research?
items.object: Apollo Research’s internal security
items.answer: By default we have been taking security quite seriously. This is because when we interact with the frontier AI companies, we don’t want to be the weakest link in the chain. For example, if we do get access to say GPT-5 before release, we get hacked, then somebody else has an API key, and that obviously would cause a problem or potentially could cause a problem, maybe not directly. So we’re quite serious about reducing the attack surface for anyone, and I think in the future this will only continue to be the case. For example, if eventually we were to evaluate internally deployed models with less guardrails, you would want to make sure that you’re in fact very resistant to potential infiltrations and external attacks and so on. So we’re already taking it very seriously, but we’re trying to upgrade even further.

items.question: How would you recommend someone build the skills to contribute to anti-scheming research?
items.object: Training and upskilling for anti-scheming research
items.answer: I’m not aware of anything right now. I think there are maybe lectures, like individual lectures or individual blog posts and series and so on, but nothing that really tries to distil the best parts and then turn that into something that people could easily consume. In general, I would strongly recommend to get your hands dirty quite quickly, and try to join, for example, some of these upskilling programmes like MATS or ARENA that often have projects that are also related to scheming in some way. For example, in my MATS stream right now we’re building black box monitors for scheming, where you try to look at the actions, and maybe the chain of thought, of the model, and try to determine whether this model was scheming or not. We’re basically just trying to improve that. And I think a lot of people would benefit very heavily by having a one- to six-month programme like this and kind of get all the basics. Then I think it’s much easier for them for example to contribute independently or join one of the companies.

items.question: How do you assess the allocation of effort across AI safety research areas such as anti-scheming, mechanistic interpretability, capability evaluations, and scalable oversight?
items.object: The allocation of effort across AI safety research areas
items.answer: First of all, I would say all of them are drastically under-represented. I think basically we could easily absorb 100 times more people into AI safety, and there would still be a lot of work to do. So all of them are, in an absolute sense, under-appreciated and underfunded. But relatively speaking, I would say mechanistic interpretability and capability evaluations are probably slightly overrepresented compared to scheming and other things. With scalable oversight, I think it’s very hard to say. Right now there is very little positive evidence that scalable oversight actually works, but it could be very valuable in the future. So it’s more like a high-risk, high-reward bet of people trying to make it work without succeeding yet.

items.object: AI control research
