items.question: How do you weigh working on AI anti-scheming inside a frontier AI lab against working at an external organisation like Apollo Research?
items.object: Working on AI anti-scheming inside a frontier AI lab versus an external organisation like Apollo Research
items.answer: I would say both are easily justifiable, and it depends a lot on your beliefs and preferences and skills. I think the case for joining a lab in a company would be you have access to the frontier models, it is easier for you to fine-tune them, it is easier for you to immediately implement mitigations. So you have very direct access to these models. The argument for external companies or external organisations like Apollo is more like… Revealed preference for me I guess is being outside. And I think there are a couple of reasons. One is we are able to work with all frontier labs, not just one, which obviously has a higher chance of impact. And we do in fact collaborate very closely with all of them, and try to influence them to make more progress on anti-scheming measures. I also think, just in general, for almost everything, that being in a very small, agile organisation with very high talent density just means you can move very fast, and within a year or so you will have more impact than at any given large organisation. At least that’s the upside. You also have a higher risk of achieving nothing. But if you’re willing to flip a bunch of coins and take risks, then I think being external typically has higher expected impact. And I think we also see that in practice. Just because we are able to move very fast, we have very little overhead within the organisation, there’s little bureaucracy, there is no politics, there is none of these other things that often slow you down in other organisations. I’m not sure how easy it is for you within a lab to communicate exactly what you think to the rest of the world, and how strongly this is restricted. I think this is also very different between the different labs. But at least if I’m in my own organisation externally, then it’s much easier for me to say exactly what I think, which is often a benefit.

items.question: How do you assess frontier AI labs’ appetite for tackling AI scheming?
items.object: Frontier AI labs’ appetite for tackling AI scheming
items.answer: The appetite so far is surprisingly high. We are talking to all of the frontier labs and they are all trying to work on scheming. And also, just to be super clear, the project with OpenAI was from their perspective a science project, not a “we care about o1” or “we realise that o1 has higher deception rates and therefore we need to implement mitigation.” So we at no point were pressured to implement something for the customer models or something like this, and they explicitly thought of it as a separate project — which I think is good, because it means they genuinely care about scheming, rather than this being a short opportunistic stint in order to get the production models to be slightly more honest. But yeah, I think the three frontier labs right now are all starting to think more about control. They’re all starting to take scheming at least a little bit more seriously as a potential failure mode. I think there are differences in terms of when they think that would be an actual problem, but all are starting to track where we are in terms of scheming capabilities and propensities.

items.question: Why do you think now is the best time to study AI scheming?
items.object: The closing window for research on AI scheming
items.answer: I think the fact that we’re potentially in a closing window with respect to scheming. Right now we’re in a position where the AI models are just barely capable enough that they show these kinds of behaviours and we can study them in detail. The chain of thought is still mostly interpretable. And in the future we may not see the chain of thought anymore, or it may be less interpretable, and the systems are significantly smarter, so the stakes are higher and they might be better at tricking you. The best time to run a really big science of scheming research programme right now is immediately and not at some point in the future. And I think the urgency is high, because we are fighting against time to some extent. So I would strongly urge people to consider thinking about how they could contribute to scheming. There are a lot of experiments to run, there are a lot of models to study, and there are many different ways in which you could do that — through direct empirical understanding, through theoretical contributions about threat modelling and how you expect AI to go wrong, through monitoring and control. There are like a bajillion things you could be doing, and I think now is the best time basically to study it.
